content: The Montana Meth Project is an anti-drug organization based in Montana, founded by billionaire Thomas Siebel. Its primary focus is an advertising campaign designed to shock and horrify viewers about the dangers of methamphetamine use. The ads often depict themes of regret, with not-yet-addicted teenagers encountering their future selves, who warn them about the devastating consequences of their choices. These advertisements frequently highlight the severe physical and psychological effects of methamphetamine use, such as amphetamine psychosis, as well as the deterioration of health and living conditions. By 2007, the campaign had expanded to other states, including Arizona and Idaho. Television Spots The Montana Meth Project's television advertisements were created by the San Francisco-based advertising agency Venables Bell & Partners. The 2005 and 2006 ads were directed by Tony Kaye, while the 2007 ads were directed by Darren Aronofsky. Below are detailed descriptions of the ads, which use the term meth as shorthand for methamphetamine. 2005-2006: Directed by Tony Kaye Phase I: Bathtub: A teenage girl is taking a shower while waiting for her friend to arrive so they can try meth for the first time. During her shower, she turns around and is horrified to see a version of herself with pockmarked, bleeding skin, shivering at the bottom of the shower. This future version of herself pleads, Don't do it. Laundromat: A young man, visibly deranged and addicted, storms into a laundromat, demanding money from everyone inside. He violently assaults a man and screams at women and children. He then confronts his pre-addicted self, grabbing him by the collar and shouting, This wasn't supposed to be your life. Just Once: A teenage girl insists she will only try meth just once. This leads to a series of escalating compromises to sustain her addiction, each time promising it will be just once. The ad ends with her younger sister stealing her drugs and whispering, I'm going to try meth, just once. That Guy: A teenage boy declares, I'm going to try meth just once. I'm not gonna be like that guy, gesturing toward a future version of himself who has deteriorated into a shaking, sweating addict on a drug dealer's couch. A teenage girl then buys meth from the same dealer, repeating the boy's earlier statement, I'm gonna try meth just once. I'm not gonna be like that guy. Phase II: Junkie Den: In a dark, grimy drug den, a young boy tries meth for the first time. He is congratulated by a group of dirty, drug-addicted individuals who welcome him as one of us. A woman promises they will shoot up together, while two men say they will steal together and we'll be sleepin' together, too. When the boy protests that he is only trying meth once, the group erupts into mocking laughter. Crash: A car is driving at night in the rain when a tire blows out, causing the vehicle to flip over. In narration, the teenage driver wishes she had crashed on her way to a party, even if it meant breaking her neck and becoming paralyzed, because it would have prevented her from trying meth. The ad cuts to her current life as an addict, smoking meth in a filthy, dilapidated apartment, where she laments, Now this is my life. Everything Else: A teenage girl approaches a group of meth users and asks for some meth. The dealer hands her the drug but also gives her everything else that comes with it. This includes an intimidating drug dealer, abusive meth boyfriends who rape her and supply her with meth, an addicted baby, and her own reflection in a mirror, showing her face disfigured by meth use. Jumped: A younger teenage boy is chased through a parking lot by three older males who beat him to the ground and kick him. In narration, the boy wishes he had been assaulted that night, as it would have prevented him from trying meth. The scene cuts to a drug den, where the boy, now addicted and trembling, says, Now all I do is meth. 2007: Directed by Darren Aronofsky Phase III: Boyfriend: A teenage girl is shown lying on a motel bed in her underwear as an older man zips up his pants and leaves the room. In narration, she says, I love my boyfriend. We've been together since like 8th grade. He takes care of me. As the older man exits, he hands something to her boyfriend, who is waiting outside the door. The boyfriend enters the room and shows her the meth, as she cringes and cries. Mother: A teenage boy is seen rummaging through his mother's purse for money. In narration, he expresses how much he loves her. When his mother enters the room and confronts him, visibly upset and concerned, he strikes her, knocking her to the floor. She clings to his leg, sobbing, but he kicks her off and flees, leaving her crying on the ground. Friends: Inside a car, two worried passengers are shown alongside a reckless driver. A female narrator says she is tight with her friends who always look out for me. The narrator is revealed to be a third passenger, slumped and unresponsive in the backseat. The car pulls up to a hospital emergency room, where her friends dump her body on the curb and drive away. Parents: In narration, he reflects on how close he used to be with his parents. Inside the house, his parents are panicked and distressed, turning off the lights to avoid him. The boy kicks the door repeatedly, begging to be let in and screaming that he is going to kill them. Criticism While many members of the Montana state legislature have praised the project as a groundbreaking success—so much so that they allocated public tax dollars to fund what was previously a privately funded initiative—some residents of Montana remain skeptical about its long-term effectiveness. Critics have labeled the campaign as relying on scare tactics and have pointed out the lack of credible scientific evidence supporting the ads' efficacy. Although some surveys suggest the project has been effective, these surveys were conducted by the project itself, leading some to question their validity and to attribute the results to a broader trend of declining methamphetamine use.
